headline: Giant bluefin stack at 100 fathoms as 68-degree water holds bait tight
subhead: Jigging and stickbaits producing fish to 96 inches on the thermocline break.
body_markdown:
The Hudson Canyon is firing on all cylinders right now, with giant bluefin tuna stacked along the 100-fathom line in numbers I haven't seen since early May. Water temps hit 68.2 degrees at the canyon edge this week, creating a perfect thermocline break that's holding massive schools of bunker and sand eels — and the giants are feeding hard.

The action has been split between two distinct bites. Early morning brings explosive topwater feeds when the bunker push up against the canyon wall. These fish want big stickbaits worked aggressively through the white water. I'm talking 8-inch to 10-inch sticks, cast right into the chaos and retrieved with sharp jerks. The takes are violent — fish launching completely out of the water before the hook sets.

But here's where it gets interesting: when those surface feeds shut down around 9 AM, the fish don't disappear. They drop to the thermocline, typically 65 to 80 feet down, and that's where the jigging bite takes over. I've been running 280-gram jigs with beefed-up hooks, bouncing them right off the bottom and working them slowly through the water column. The key is finding that temperature break — the fish are sitting right on it, sometimes just 5 feet off the deck.

The 68-degree surface water we're seeing is crucial. It's creating a distinct thermal layer that's concentrating bait, and when you find that edge on your fish finder, you'll mark fish. I've been working the area from the Claw south to the Dip, focusing on the 600 to 700-foot depths where the canyon wall creates natural upwelling.

Tackle is critical for these fish. I'm running 50-80 pound class rods with quality lever-drag reels spooled with 65-pound braid to 80-pound fluorocarbon leaders. Don't cheap out on the terminal tackle — these fish will test every connection. Start your drag at 35 pounds and be ready to back it off when they make their runs.

The bite timing has been predictable: first light for the surface action, then the jig bite from 9 AM through early afternoon. Tide changes seem to trigger feeding, especially the flood tide pushing bait up the canyon walls. With the new moon approaching Friday, expect bigger tidal swings and more aggressive feeding windows.

Looking ahead, this 68-degree water should hold through the weekend if we don't get any major weather. The thermal structure is stable, and the bait is thick from the Texas Tower north to the 100-fathom line. I'm expecting the topwater bite to continue strong, especially with calm conditions forecast. The key will be getting there early — first boat on the water gets first crack at the surface feeds before the fleet arrives and pressures the fish down.
